content: The Back to Sleep initiative is a program supported by the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), which is part of the National Institutes of Health. Its primary goal is to encourage parents to place their infants to sleep on their backs, also known as the supine position, in order to reduce the risk of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS). Since the launch of the Back to Sleep campaign in 1994, the incidence of SIDS has decreased by more than 50%. In 1992, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) issued a recommendation that infants should sleep on their backs or sides to lower the risk of SIDS. However, this recommendation was revised in 1996 to emphasize that the back-sleeping position is the safest. Following this, NICHD launched the Back to Sleep campaign in 1994 to widely disseminate this message to the public. The campaign proved to be highly effective, as it significantly reduced the percentage of infants sleeping in the prone position (on their stomachs), which is associated with a higher risk of SIDS. It is important to note that infants sleeping on their stomachs are approximately twice as likely to die from SIDS compared to those sleeping on their backs. Additionally, disparities in SIDS risk exist, with certain populations, such as Black infants, being at a higher risk compared to White infants.
